--- title: "Kinds of marine data" description: "Continuous, categorical, circular, temporal, spatial, profile and compositional data, and what each one needs before a model can use it." order: 3 categories: [data-preparation, marine-data] --- ## A model sees only numbers A model does not know that `season` is a season or that `longitude` is a position. It sees numbers, and does arithmetic on them whatever they mean. This page shows the kinds of variable marine data holds and what each needs before a model can use it correctly, so you can spot a misread column before it misleads a model. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the Python tabs Most code blocks on this page have an **R** and a **Python** tab, and picking one switches the whole page. Both run when the site is built, and each tab shows its own output. The Python tab is the scikit-learn equivalent of the R; the figures come from R throughout, and a few steps with no scikit-learn counterpart have no Python tab, which is itself worth noticing. Expect the **numbers to differ slightly** where randomness is involved: R and Python draw their random splits from different generators, so the split is not the same one. The conclusions are. ::: ## Seven kinds of variable Most introductions stop at two kinds, numbers and categories. Marine data has more: ::: {.diagram} ![Seven kinds of variable common in marine data, with examples of each and what it needs before a model can use it.](img/data-kinds.svg){fig-alt="Seven cards. Continuous: temperature, depth, salinity; needs scaling. Categorical: substrate, gear type, vessel; needs encoding as numbers. Circular: month, season, bearing, tidal phase; needs sine and cosine. Temporal: sampling dates and times; needs a known date format. Spatial: longitude, latitude; needs splits by area. Profile: a CTD cast, values down the water; needs one summary per cast. Compositional: species shares, grain-size fractions; needs log-ratios."} ::: **Continuous** variables are quantities, where differences mean something; they need only a common scale, covered in [Scaling and encoding](scaling-and-encoding.qmd), which also turns **categories** into numbers. The rest of this page covers the kinds that are easy to get wrong. ## A number is not always a quantity A column stored as numbers is not necessarily a quantity. A survey year stored as an integer invites a model to conclude that 2023 is 1.0005 times 2021, and a station number is a name, not a measurement. Categories come in two kinds. **Nominal** categories have no order: sand, mud, gravel, rock. **Ordinal** categories have an order but unknown spacing: a disturbance score of low, medium or high. Coding it 1, 2, 3 claims that medium sits exactly halfway, which is a guess. ## Cycles belong on a circle Month, day of year, tidal phase, current direction and time of day all go round in a circle. December is month 12 and January month 1: eleven apart on a number line, but neighbours in the ocean. The usual fix places the cycle on a circle with two new columns, its sine and cosine: $$x_1 = \sin\!\left(\frac{2\pi t}{T}\right), \qquad x_2 = \cos\!\left(\frac{2\pi t}{T}\right)$$ where $t$ is the position in the cycle and $T$ its length: 12 for months, 365 for days of the year, 360 for a bearing. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} months <- tibble( month = 1:12, name = month.abb, x = sin(2 * pi * month / 12), y = cos(2 * pi * month / 12) ) p_line <- ggplot(months, aes(month, 0)) + geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "#d7dde2") + geom_point(size = 3, colour = ml_palette[["blue"]]) + geom_text(aes(label = name), vjust = -1.4, size = 3.2) + annotate("segment", x = 1, xend = 12, y = -0.35, yend = -0.35, colour = ml_palette[["vermilion"]], linewidth = 0.8, arrow = arrow(ends = "both", length = unit(0.15, "cm"))) + annotate("text", x = 6.5, y = -0.5, label = "the model thinks these are 11 apart", colour = ml_palette[["vermilion"]], size = 3.4) + coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-0.7, 0.5)) + scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(2, 12, 2)) + labs(x = "Month number", y = NULL, title = "As a raw number") + theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), panel.grid.major = element_blank(), panel.grid.minor = element_blank()) p_circle <- ggplot(months, aes(x, y)) + geom_path(data = tibble(x = sin(seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = 200)), y = cos(seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = 200))), colour = "#d7dde2") + geom_point(size = 3, colour = ml_palette[["blue"]]) + geom_text(aes(label = name, x = x * 1.18, y = y * 1.18), size = 3.2) + annotate("text", x = 0, y = 0, label = "Dec and Jan\nare neighbours", colour = ml_palette[["vermilion"]], size = 3.4) + coord_fixed(xlim = c(-1.35, 1.35), ylim = c(-1.35, 1.35)) + labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, title = "As sine and cosine") + theme(axis.text = element_blank(), panel.grid.major = element_blank(), panel.grid.minor = element_blank()) p_line + p_circle ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The same twelve months, encoded two ways. On a number line December and January sit at opposite ends; on a circle they are neighbours, which is what the ocean does.](marine-data-types_files/figure-html/fig-circular-1.png){#fig-circular fig-alt='Two panels. The left panel places months 1 to 12 along a straight horizontal line, with a long arrow showing the distance of 11 between December and January. The right panel places the same months around a circle, with December and January adjacent.' width=1700} ::: ::: The encoding spends two columns on one variable and assumes the cycle is smooth. A quantity that jumps at a boundary, such as a management year starting in April, does not belong on a circle. ## Dates need a known format Dates arrive as text, in whatever format the logging software wrote. The two vessels of the survey used two formats: ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} raw <- load_coastal_survey_raw() raw |> distinct(vessel, sample_date) |> slice_head(n = 2, by = vessel) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|vessel |sample_date | |:----------|:-----------| |RV Kaiyo |2022-04-21 | |RV Kaiyo |2022-10-21 | |RV Tsubasa |05/10/2022 | |RV Tsubasa |15/01/2019 |
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} import pandas as pd from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_survey_raw raw = load_coastal_survey_raw() raw[["vessel", "sample_date"]].drop_duplicates().groupby("vessel").head(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | | vessel | sample_date | |---:|:-----------|:--------------| | 0 | RV Kaiyo | 2022-04-21 | | 1 | RV Kaiyo | 2022-10-21 | | 3 | RV Tsubasa | 05/10/2022 | | 6 | RV Tsubasa | 15/01/2019 | ::: ::: ::: A date such as `05/10/2022` is 5 October in most of the world and 10 May in the United States, and nothing in the text says which. Read the wrong way, it moves a station into another season without any error. So find out which format each source used, and parse each format explicitly: ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dated <- raw |> mutate( sample_date = coalesce(ymd(sample_date, quiet = TRUE), dmy(sample_date, quiet = TRUE)), day_of_year = yday(sample_date) ) sum(is.na(dated$sample_date)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> [1] 0 ``` ::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} # One vessel logged ISO dates, the other day-first. Parse each format on its # own and take whichever succeeded, rather than letting pandas guess per row. iso = pd.to_datetime(raw["sample_date"], format="%Y-%m-%d", errors="coerce") dayfirst = pd.to_datetime(raw["sample_date"], format="%d/%m/%Y", errors="coerce") dated = raw.assign(sample_date=iso.fillna(dayfirst)) dated["day_of_year"] = dated["sample_date"].dt.dayofyear int(dated["sample_date"].isna().sum()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> 0 ``` ::: ::: ::: Every date parsed, and `day_of_year` is ready for the sine and cosine above. ## Time and position are mostly structure Time and position can be features, but they matter more as **structure**: they say which observations are close to each other, and so likely to be alike. Samples a day apart, or a few kilometres apart, share information, as repeat visits to a site do ([The coastal survey](the-coastal-survey.qmd#the-stations-come-from-far-fewer-sites)). That limits how the data can be split to test a model, which [Splitting the data](splitting-data.qmd) takes up. Used as features, longitude and latitude often improve predictions while explaining nothing, because they stand in for whatever the other columns missed, just as salinity stood in for depth in [Prediction and explanation](../01-introduction/prediction-and-explanation.qmd). Physical variables built from position, such as distance to the coast or the slope of the seabed, are usually more useful than raw coordinates. ## Profiles and shares need reshaping A **profile**, such as a CTD cast, is a curve down the water, not a single row. The usual start is one row per cast with summaries chosen for the biology: surface temperature, mixed layer depth, total chlorophyll. Splitting the cast into one row per depth band instead multiplies rows that are not independent, so a cast's rows must be kept together when the data is split. **Compositional** data, such as the share of each species in a sample, sums to one: if one share rises, others must fall. Methods that ignore this can report relationships that come from the arithmetic, not the ecology. Log-ratio transformations are the usual remedy. ## The kinds in the survey The raw survey file mixes five of the seven kinds in its 17 columns: ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} tibble( column = names(raw), stored_as = map_chr(raw, \(x) class(x)[1]) ) |> mutate(really = case_when( column %in% c("station_id", "site_id", "vessel", "substrate", "present", "rare_species") ~ "categorical", column == "season" ~ "circular", column == "sample_date" ~ "temporal (as text)", column == "survey_year" ~ "temporal, not a quantity", column %in% c("longitude", "latitude") ~ "spatial", column %in% c("abundance", "catch_weight_kg") ~ "outcome", TRUE ~ "continuous" )) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|column |stored_as |really | |:-----------------|:---------|:------------------------| |station_id |character |categorical | |site_id |character |categorical | |vessel |character |categorical | |sample_date |character |temporal (as text) | |survey_year |integer |temporal, not a quantity | |season |character |circular | |longitude |numeric |spatial | |latitude |numeric |spatial | |depth_m |numeric |continuous | |temperature_c |numeric |continuous | |salinity_psu |numeric |continuous | |chlorophyll_mg_m3 |numeric |continuous | |substrate |character |categorical | |abundance |integer |outcome | |catch_weight_kg |numeric |outcome | |present |character |categorical | |rare_species |character |categorical |
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} categorical = ["station_id", "site_id", "vessel", "substrate", "present", "rare_species"] def really(column): if column in categorical: return "categorical" if column == "season": return "circular" if column == "sample_date": return "temporal (as text)" if column == "survey_year": return "temporal, not a quantity" if column in ("longitude", "latitude"): return "spatial" if column in ("abundance", "catch_weight_kg"): return "outcome" return "continuous" pd.DataFrame({ "column": raw.columns, "stored_as": [raw[c].dtype.name for c in raw.columns], "really": [really(c) for c in raw.columns], }) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | column | stored_as | really | |:------------------|:------------|:-------------------------| | station_id | str | categorical | | site_id | str | categorical | | vessel | str | categorical | | sample_date | str | temporal (as text) | | survey_year | int64 | temporal, not a quantity | | season | str | circular | | longitude | float64 | spatial | | latitude | float64 | spatial | | depth_m | float64 | continuous | | temperature_c | float64 | continuous | | salinity_psu | float64 | continuous | | chlorophyll_mg_m3 | float64 | continuous | | substrate | str | categorical | | abundance | int64 | outcome | | catch_weight_kg | float64 | outcome | | present | str | categorical | | rare_species | str | categorical | ::: ::: ::: Two columns are easy to misread. `survey_year` is stored as a number but is not a quantity. `season` is stored as text, and treating it as four unrelated categories throws away the fact that spring comes between winter and summer. No inspection of the file reveals either: knowing what a column means is knowledge you bring. ## Key points ::: {.key-points} - A model does arithmetic on whatever it is given; stored as a number does not make a column a quantity. - Circular variables such as month, bearing and tidal phase need sine and cosine, or December ends up far from January. - Ambiguous date formats silently move stations between seasons: know the format and parse it explicitly. - Time and position are mostly structure: they say which rows are alike, which limits how the data can be split. - Profiles need summarising, usually one row per cast; compositional shares need log-ratios. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Encode `day_of_year` as sine and cosine, and plot `abundance` against each. Does the seasonal pattern look clearer than against `season` as four categories? 2. List the columns in your own data and write next to each what it *means*, not how it is stored. How many are circular, compositional, or a name stored as a number?
